lines.text: The gates of {name} are closed. There are people on the walls. This is not the relaxed watch of a settlement going about its day. These are people watching the treeline. A runner comes out of the small side gate, sees your group, stops.

{name}'s gates are open but attended: every person entering is noted, every cart searched. The guards are professional about it, which makes it worse. Professional means this has been happening long enough to become routine.

lines.text: From the road, {name} looks ordinary. Smoke from cookfires, the sound of a market. It is only at the gate that the weight becomes apparent: the guards' expressions, the way conversation stops when strangers approach.

lines.text: The approach to {name} is quieter than it should be for a settlement this size. The outlying farms are empty. The road has not been maintained recently. The settlement itself is intact, but everything around it has been abandoned to the walls.
The fields around {name} were harvested early and badly: stubble cut in haste, carts gone. Whatever the walls are waiting for, the granaries inside are already keeping its schedule.
A thrown stone sits half-buried a hundred paces short of {name}'s wall, left where it landed. Nobody has hauled it away. There are fresher things to attend to.
{name} has drawn in on itself. Every family from the outlying fields is sleeping under a neighbour's roof, the livestock are penned between the houses, and someone is always watching the treeline.
There are campfires on the hill above {name}, and they are not {name}'s. The people inside keep their own fires low and their voices lower, and they count the strangers' fires every night.
Carts and timber block the lanes into {name}, piled in a hurry and manned around the clock. The faces behind them are farmers' faces, and none of them has slept.

{name} gets by. The market is busy enough, the streets clean enough and the civic buildings kept up just enough, and nothing more is being spent.

lines.text: The approach to {name} is interrupted by a checkpoint a quarter mile from the gates: a temporary structure, manned by people wearing cloth over their faces. They want to know where you came from and when.

{name}'s gate is open, the market is running, and there are people in the street. People are giving each other slightly more space than usual. A cart passes with barrels marked with an unfamiliar symbol. You have seen that symbol once before, on a quarantine notice.
Near the gate of {name} there is a temporary shelter: a healer's station, by the look of it, with two attendants and a queue. The queue is not yet long. That is either good or early.

Some of {name}'s market stalls are closed. Not all, not most, but several, in a pattern that isn't about the day of the week. The ones that are open are busy; the ones that are closed have been for a while.
{name}'s gate stands open, but the gatekeeper waves you through from a distance, and the well just inside has been roped off under a painted sign too weathered to read from horseback.
Smoke rises from {name} at midday: not cookfires but something being burned deliberately, bedding or clothes, in a yard behind the healer's house. The street watches it burn and says nothing.
{name} smells of vinegar and woodsmoke. Doors that should be open are shut, and the people who do come out keep a careful distance from one another, and from you.

lines.text: {name} has grown a second settlement outside its walls: tents and lean-tos and cookfires on the ground that used to be common pasture. The people there watch you approach with the wariness of those who arrived too late to get inside.

Half of {name} seems to have arrived this year. You pass loaded wagons on the road heading in, and inside the walls every spare room has a family in it. Those who were here first have the look of people deciding how much more they can give.

{name}'s market speaks three languages you can pick out and more you cannot. The old families and the newcomers trade at the same stalls and do not quite look at each other. Everyone is doing business. No one is comfortable.
The road to {name} has acquired a verge of graves: recent, orderly, unmarked but tended. People arrived here in numbers, and not all of them finished the journey.
{name}'s smithy has a queue for wheel-rims and none for ploughshares. A town where the carts outnumber the fields is a town still filling with people who came here with everything they own.
